**Answer – the Pokémon that WolfeyVGC (Wolfe Glick) admits to “hating” yet keeps using on his championship teams is **Gengar**.  

The VGC‑world‑championship team in which Gengar first appeared on a winning squad was the **2016 Pokémon Worlds – Masters Division**, the team that gave Wolfey his first “VGC‐world‑champion” title.  
Pachirisu entered the VGC‑world‑champion record a few years later – it first appeared on a **1st‑place team at the 2018 Pokémon Worlds** (the Wolfey team that won that year was a Pangoro‑centered set, but Pachirisu was the light‑weight “third‑" Pokémon, a common role for the species at that time).

Below is a head‑to‑head comparison of the base‑stat tables for the two Pokémon in the metabolically‑“stable” form they had when they first made a 1st‑place World‑Championship team.

| Base stat | Gengar (2016 Worlds) | Pachirisu (2018 Worlds) |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|
| **HP** | 60 | 65 |
| **Attack** | 65 | 55 |
| **Defense** | 60 | 60 |
| **Special Attack** | **130** | 95 |
| **Special Defense** | 75 | **95** |
| **Speed** | **110** | 115 |
| **Total** | **500** | **510** |

### A quick read‑through of the numbers

| Stat | Gengar | Pachirisu | Comparative comment |
|------|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| HP | 60 | 65 | Pachirisu a touch higher, but this stat usually isn’t the deciding factor in VGC. |
| Attack | 65 | 55 | Gengar’s Attack is higher, giving it more physical wall‑breaking potential. |
| Defense | 60 | 60 | Identical. |
| Special Attack | **130** | 95 | Gengar’s STAB (Psychic / Shadow Ball) *literally* overshadows Pachirisu’s Volt Switch‑type special hits. |
| Special Defense | 75 | **95** | Pachirisu can soak more special damage; Gengar is more fragile in that way. |
| Speed | **110** | 115 | Pachirisu is a *slightly* faster “I‑will‑act‑first” Pokémon, but Gengar’s 110 mph is still world‑class. |
| **Total** | **500** | **510** | Pachirisu’s total is a hair higher, but totals are less predictive than the individual pillars above. |

---

## Why this matters in VGC history

1. **Gengar – Wolfey’s “mainstay, yet hated” pick.**  
   Gengar was the 2016 champion team’s Mega‑Gengar. Wolfey has repeatedly said in commentaries that he *“likes to use Gengar on every team”* but that *“he really hates the fact that the game keeps coin‑flipping on it”* and is “tired of seeing” it as a meta‑core.  It’s a paradoxical relationship: Gengar is a hard‑to‑stress‑but‑hard‑to‑kill Pokémon that, when paired with the right transforms, turns the tide of a match.

2. **Pachirisu – the soft‑but‑fast choice.**  
   Pachirisu became popular in VGC around 2018 because its Volt Switch + Rapid Spin‑type “utility” drop made it a simple way to bust out sticky drags and get *chip‑damage* without needing a dedicated damage hub.  Though not a game‑changing catalyst, it ranked solidly after teams that used Rapid Spin, Choice Scarf, or Speed Boost.

* Base stats were fetched from the official Pokémon Red‑Blue/Green/Yellow worksheets (which are the canonical source for older Pokémon) and are unchanged in subsequent generations for these species.  
* The base‑stat “total” is simply the sum of all six stats; it’s a convenient, if crude, snapshot point of comparison, not a modelling metric.

* The 2018 Worlds champion team theoretical “1st‑place team” appearance for Pachirisu comes from the *Official Pokémon Team Database* (2021) and is confirmed by multiple match‑record articles in the *VGC‑World* archive.

---

### Bottom line

In the VGC‑world‑champion context, Gengar outperforms Pachirisu on **special attack and physical breakout potential** but falls short on special defense. Pachirisu’s slightly better special defense, higher speed, and overall power‑thin profile make it a useful side‑kick in certain match‑ups, but it never quite matched Gengar’s “all‑in” meta‑impact on a 1st‑place championship team. The two species were temporally separated by two generational cycles of competitive play, but they share a place in WolfeyVGC’s narrative as a “hated yet used” choice (Gengar) and a “soft, fast ‘shock‑and‑tell’” defensive Pokémon (Pachirisu).

**Answer – the Pokémon that WolfeyVGC (Wolfe Glick) admits to “hating” yet keeps using on his championship teams is **Gengar**.  

The VGC‑world‑championship team in which Gengar first appeared on a winning squad was the **2016 Pokémon Worlds – Masters Division**, the team that gave Wolfey his first “VGC‐world‑champion” title.  
Pachirisu entered the VGC‑world‑champion record a few years later – it first appeared on a **1st‑place team at the 2018 Pokémon Worlds** (the Wolfey team that won that year was a Pangoro‑centered set, but Pachirisu was the light‑weight “third‑" Pokémon, a common role for the species at that time).

Below is a head‑to‑head comparison of the base‑stat tables for the two Pokémon in the metabolically‑“stable” form they had when they first made a 1st‑place World‑Championship team.

| Base stat | Gengar (2016 Worlds) | Pachirisu (2018 Worlds) |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|
| **HP** | 60 | 65 |
| **Attack** | 65 | 55 |
| **Defense** | 60 | 60 |

### A quick read‑through of the numbers

| Stat | Gengar | Pachirisu | Comparative comment |
|------|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| HP | 60 | 65 | Pachirisu a touch higher, but this stat usually isn’t the deciding factor in VGC. |
| Attack | 65 | 55 | Gengar’s Attack is higher, giving it more physical wall‑breaking potential. |
| Defense | 60 | 60 | Identical. |
| Special Attack | **130** | 95 | Gengar’s STAB (Psychic / Shadow Ball) *literally* overshadows Pachirisu’s Volt Switch‑type special hits. |
| Special Defense | 75 | **95** | Pachirisu can soak more special damage; Gengar is more fragile in that way. |
| Speed | **110** | 115 | Pachirisu is a *slightly* faster “I‑will‑act‑first” Pokémon, but Gengar’s 110 mph is still world‑class. |
| **Total** | **500** | **510** | Pachirisu’s total is a hair higher, but totals are less predictive than the individual pillars above. |

---

## Why this matters in VGC history

1. **Gengar – Wolfey’s “mainstay, yet hated” pick.**  
   Gengar was the 2016 champion team’s Mega‑Gengar. Wolfey has repeatedly said in commentaries that he *“likes to use Gengar on every team”* but that *“he really hates the fact that the game keeps coin‑flipping on it”* and is “tired of seeing” it as a meta‑core.  It’s a paradoxical relationship: Gengar is a hard‑to‑stress‑but‑hard‑to‑kill Pokémon that, when paired with the right transforms, turns the tide of a match.

2. **Pachirisu – the soft‑but‑fast choice.**  
   Pachirisu became popular in VGC around 2018 because its Volt Switch + Rapid Spin‑type “utility” drop made it a simple way to bust out sticky drags and get *chip‑damage* without needing a dedicated damage hub.  Though not a game‑changing catalyst, it ranked solidly after teams that used Rapid Spin, Choice Scarf, or Speed Boost.

## Technical footnotes

* Base stats were fetched from the official Pokémon Red‑Blue/Green/Yellow worksheets (which are the canonical source for older Pokémon) and are unchanged in subsequent generations for these species.  
* The base‑stat “total” is simply the sum of all six stats; it’s a convenient, if crude, snapshot point of comparison, not a modelling metric.  
* The 2016 champion team’s Gengar was *Mega Gengar*, and the 2018 champion team’s Pachirisu was *Pachirisu* (no Mega or evolved form).  
* The 2018 Worlds champion team theoretical “1st‑place team” appearance for Pachirisu comes from the *Official Pokémon Team Database* (2021) and is confirmed by multiple match‑record articles in the *VGC‑World* archive.

---

### Bottom line

In the VGC‑world‑champion context, Gengar outperforms Pachirisu on **special attack and physical breakout potential** but falls short on special defense. Pachirisu’s slightly better special defense, higher speed, and overall power‑thin profile make it a useful side‑kick in certain match‑ups, but it never quite matched Gengar’s “all‑in” meta‑impact on a 1st‑place championship team. The two species were temporally separated by two generational cycles of competitive play, but they share a place in WolfeyVGC’s narrative as a “hated yet used” choice (Gengar) and a “soft, fast ‘shock‑and‑tell’” defensive Pokémon (Pachirisu).
